rows.stem: If \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 3ax - b, & x > 1 \\ 11, & x = 1 \\ -5ax - 2b, & x < 1 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 1\), then the values of a and b are :
rows.solution:
Continuity at \(x = 1\) needs the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value \(f(1)\) all to agree. Since each branch is a polynomial, the one-sided limits are found by substituting \(x = 1\) into the relevant branch:
\(\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} f(x) = 3a(1) - b = 3a - b\), \(\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} f(x) = -5a(1) - 2b = -5a - 2b\), and \(f(1) = 11\).
Setting each equal to \(11\) gives two equations:
\(3a - b = 11\)  ...(i)
\(-5a - 2b = 11\)  ...(ii)
From (i), \(b = 3a - 11\). Substituting into (ii),
\(-5a - 2(3a - 11) = 11 \Rightarrow -5a - 6a + 22 = 11 \Rightarrow -11a = -11 \Rightarrow a = 1\),
and then \(b = 3(1) - 11 = -8\).
So the values are \(a = 1\), \(b = -8\).
Check: \(3(1) - (-8) = 11\) and \(-5(1) - 2(-8) = -5 + 16 = 11\), both equal to \(f(1)\). (Each of the other three pairs fails the first equation — for instance \(a = 3\), \(b = 5\) gives \(3(3) - 5 = 4 \ne 11\).)

rows.stem: Edge of a variable cube increases at the rate of 5 cm/s. The rate at which the surface area of the cube increases when the edge is 2 cm long is :
rows.solution:
This is a related-rates question, so differentiate the surface-area formula with respect to TIME and substitute at the required instant.
Let the edge of the cube be \(a\) cm at time \(t\) seconds. Its total surface area is
\(S = 6a^2\).
Differentiating with respect to \(t\) by the chain rule,
\(\frac{dS}{dt} = 12a\,\frac{da}{dt}\).
We are given \(\frac{da}{dt} = 5\) cm/s, and we want the rate when \(a = 2\) cm. So
\(\frac{dS}{dt} = 12 \times 2 \times 5 = 120\).
Hence the surface area is increasing at \(120\ \mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{s}\).
(The value \(24\) is the surface area \(6a^2\) itself at \(a = 2\), not a rate, and \(12\) is \(12a\) without the factor \(\frac{da}{dt}\).)

The numerator \(e^{-x}\) is, up to sign, the derivative of \(e^{-x}\), and \(e^{-2x} = \left(e^{-x}\right)^2\) — that pairing points straight to a substitution.
Put \(t = e^{-x}\), so \(dt = -e^{-x}dx\), i.e. \(e^{-x}dx = -dt\), and \(9e^{-2x} = 9t^2\). Then
\(\int \frac{e^{-x}}{16 + 9e^{-2x}}\,dx = -\int \frac{dt}{16 + 9t^2} = -\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{dt}{\frac{16}{9} + t^2}\).
Using \(\int \frac{dt}{k^2 + t^2} = \frac{1}{k}\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{k}\) with \(k = \frac{4}{3}\),
\(= -\frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{3}{4}\tan^{-1}\frac{3t}{4} + C = -\frac{1}{12}\tan^{-1}\frac{3t}{4} + C\).
Restoring \(t = e^{-x}\),
\(\int \frac{e^{-x}}{16 + 9e^{-2x}}\,dx = -\frac{1}{12}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3e^{-x}}{4}\right) + C\),
which is the choice \(-\frac{1}{12}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3e^{-x}}{4}\right) + C\).
(The minus sign comes from \(dt = -e^{-x}dx\) and must not be dropped; the forms carrying \(\frac{e^{-x}}{4}\) inside the arctangent would come from \(16 + e^{-2x}\), which is not the given denominator.)

rows.stem: If A and B are two events such that \(P(B) = \dfrac{1}{5}\), \(P(A\ |\ B) = \dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{3}{5}\), then \(P(A)\) is :
rows.solution:
First convert the conditional probability into an intersection. By definition \(P(A\,|\,B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\), so
\(P(A \cap B) = P(A\,|\,B)\cdot P(B) = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{5} = \frac{2}{15}\).
Now use the addition theorem, rearranged to isolate \(P(A)\):
\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \Rightarrow P(A) = P(A \cup B) + P(A \cap B) - P(B)\).
Substituting the three known values,
\(P(A) = \frac{3}{5} + \frac{2}{15} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{9}{15} + \frac{2}{15} - \frac{3}{15} = \frac{8}{15}\).
So \(P(A) = \frac{8}{15}\).
(As a sanity check, \(P(A \cap B) = \frac{2}{15}\) does not exceed either \(P(A) = \frac{8}{15}\) or \(P(B) = \frac{3}{15}\), as an intersection must not. The value \(\frac{2}{15}\) is the intersection itself, and \(\frac{1}{5}\) is \(P(B)\).)

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), then find the value of K if \(A^2 = 6A + KI_2\), where \(I_2\) is an identity matrix.
rows.solution:
First compute \(A^2\):
\(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1(1) + 0(-1) & 1(0) + 0(5) \\ -1(1) + 5(-1) & -1(0) + 5(5) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -6 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\).
Next build the right-hand side:
\(6A + KI_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ -6 & 30 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} K & 0 \\ 0 & K \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 + K & 0 \\ -6 & 30 + K \end{bmatrix}\).
Two matrices are equal only when every corresponding entry is equal. Comparing the \((1,1)\) entries,
\(6 + K = 1 \Rightarrow K = -5\).
This must be consistent with the other entries, and it is: the \((2,2)\) entries give \(30 + K = 25 \Rightarrow K = -5\), the same value, while the \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) entries read \(0 = 0\) and \(-6 = -6\) regardless of K.
Hence \(K = -5\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
For a Linear Programming Problem, find min \(Z = 5x + 3y\) (where Z is the objective function) for the feasible region shaded in the given figure.

(Note : The figure is not to scale)
rows.figure: REQUIRED - the stem gives the objective function ONLY; every constraint lives in the printed graph. The figure shades a triangle with vertices labelled A, B and C bounded by the lines x + 3y = 9 and x + y = 5 and the y-axis, and carries the printed caveat that it is not to scale. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Read the constraints off the printed figure: the shaded region is the triangle bounded by the line \(x + 3y = 9\), the line \(x + y = 5\) and the y-axis, with the three vertices marked A, B and C.
Find those vertices by intersecting the boundaries in pairs.
C is where \(x + 3y = 9\) meets the y-axis: putting \(x = 0\) gives \(3y = 9\), so \(C(0, 3)\).
B is where \(x + y = 5\) meets the y-axis: putting \(x = 0\) gives \(B(0, 5)\).
A is where the two lines cross: subtracting \(x + y = 5\) from \(x + 3y = 9\) gives \(2y = 4\), so \(y = 2\) and \(x = 3\), i.e. \(A(3, 2)\).
The region is a triangle and hence BOUNDED, so by the corner-point method the optimum of a linear objective function is attained at a vertex. Evaluating \(Z = 5x + 3y\):
at \(A(3, 2)\): \(Z = 5(3) + 3(2) = 15 + 6 = 21\);
at \(B(0, 5)\): \(Z = 5(0) + 3(5) = 15\);
at \(C(0, 3)\): \(Z = 5(0) + 3(3) = 9\).
The smallest of these is \(9\), so the minimum value is
\(\text{Min } Z = 9\), attained at the corner point \(C(0, 3)\).

rows.stem: Differentiate \(\log (x^x + \mathrm{cosec}^2 x)\) with respect to x.
rows.solution:
Differentiate the logarithm by the chain rule, then handle the two terms inside it separately — the second term is straightforward, but \(x^x\) has the variable in BOTH the base and the exponent, so it needs the exponential form.
Write \(x^x = e^{x\log x}\) (valid for \(x > 0\)). Then
\(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^x\right) = e^{x\log x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(x\log x\right) = e^{x\log x}\left(\log x + x \cdot \frac{1}{x}\right) = x^x\left(1 + \log x\right)\).
For the other term, using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\mathrm{cosec}\,x\right) = -\mathrm{cosec}\,x \cot x\),
\(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\mathrm{cosec}^2 x\right) = 2\,\mathrm{cosec}\,x \cdot \left(-\mathrm{cosec}\,x\cot x\right) = -2\,\mathrm{cosec}^2 x\cot x\).
Now apply \(\frac{d}{dx}\log u = \frac{1}{u}\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u = x^x + \mathrm{cosec}^2 x\):
\(\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(x^x + \mathrm{cosec}^2 x\right) = \frac{1}{x^x + \mathrm{cosec}^2 x}\left[x^x\left(1 + \log x\right) - 2\,\mathrm{cosec}^2 x\cot x\right]\).
That is the required derivative.

rows.stem: Show that of all the rectangles with a fixed perimeter, the square has the greatest area.
rows.solution:
Let the rectangle have sides \(x\) and \(y\), and let its perimeter be the FIXED constant P. Then
\(2(x + y) = P \Rightarrow y = \frac{P - 2x}{2}\),
so the area can be written as a function of the single variable \(x\):
\(A(x) = xy = x \cdot \frac{P - 2x}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(Px - 2x^2\right)\), for \(0 < x < \frac{P}{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(A'(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left(P - 4x\right)\).
Setting \(A'(x) = 0\) gives
\(P - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{P}{4}\), and then \(y = \frac{P - 2 \cdot \frac{P}{4}}{2} = \frac{P - \frac{P}{2}}{2} = \frac{P}{4}\).
For the second-derivative test,
\(A''(x) = \frac{1}{2}(-4) = -2 < 0\)
for every \(x\), and in particular at \(x = \frac{P}{4}\), so this critical point gives a MAXIMUM (and, the second derivative being negative throughout, it is the absolute maximum on the interval).
Since \(x = y = \frac{P}{4}\), the rectangle of greatest area is the one with all four sides equal — a square. Its area is \(\frac{P^2}{16}\).
Hence, of all rectangles with a fixed perimeter, the square has the greatest area.

The denominator is already factorised, with \((x - 2)\) REPEATED, so the partial-fraction form needs a term for each power of the repeated factor:
\(\frac{3x + 1}{(x - 2)^2 (x + 2)} = \frac{A}{x - 2} + \frac{B}{(x - 2)^2} + \frac{C}{x + 2}\).
Multiplying through by \((x - 2)^2(x + 2)\),
\(3x + 1 = A(x - 2)(x + 2) + B(x + 2) + C(x - 2)^2\).
Put \(x = 2\): \(7 = B(4)\), so \(B = \frac{7}{4}\).
Put \(x = -2\): \(-5 = C(16)\), so \(C = -\frac{5}{16}\).
Comparing the coefficients of \(x^2\): \(0 = A + C\), so \(A = -C = \frac{5}{16}\).
Therefore
\(\int \frac{3x + 1}{(x - 2)^2(x + 2)}\,dx = \frac{5}{16}\int \frac{dx}{x - 2} + \frac{7}{4}\int \frac{dx}{(x - 2)^2} - \frac{5}{16}\int \frac{dx}{x + 2}\).
The first and third are logarithms; the middle one uses \(\int (x - 2)^{-2}dx = -\frac{1}{x - 2}\). Hence
\(= \frac{5}{16}\log|x - 2| - \frac{7}{4(x - 2)} - \frac{5}{16}\log|x + 2| + C\),
which may also be written as
\(\frac{5}{16}\log\left|\frac{x - 2}{x + 2}\right| - \frac{7}{4(x - 2)} + C\).

The limits \(0\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) with a lone \(x\) in the numerator point to the property \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx\).
Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{x}{\cos x + \sin x}\,dx\). Replacing \(x\) by \(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\), and using \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin x\), \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x\) — so the DENOMINATOR is unchanged —
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\frac{\pi}{2} - x}{\sin x + \cos x}\,dx\).
Adding the two expressions, the term in \(x\) cancels:
\(2I = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{\cos x + \sin x}\).
Now write the denominator as a single cosine: \(\cos x + \sin x = \sqrt{2}\cos\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). Hence
\(2I = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sec\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)dx \Rightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sec\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)dx\).
Using \(\int \sec u\,du = \log|\sec u + \tan u|\),
\(I = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}\left[\log\left|\sec\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) + \tan\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\).
At \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) the bracket is \(\sec\frac{\pi}{4} + \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt{2} + 1\); at \(x = 0\) it is \(\sec\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + \tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2} - 1\). Therefore
\(I = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}\left[\log\left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right) - \log\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)\right] = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{2} + 1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}\right)\).
Rationalising the fraction inside the logarithm gives \(\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{\sqrt{2}-1} = \left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)^2\), so the answer may equally be written \(I = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right)\), which is about \(0\cdot979\).

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation \((x - \sin y)\, dy + (\tan y)\, dx = 0\), given \(y(0) = 0\).
rows.solution:
As it stands the equation is awkward in \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), but treating \(x\) as the DEPENDENT variable and \(y\) as the independent one turns it into a standard linear equation.
From \((x - \sin y)\,dy + \tan y\,dx = 0\),
\(\tan y\,\frac{dx}{dy} = \sin y - x \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{\sin y - x}{\tan y} = \cos y - x\cot y\),
since \(\frac{\sin y}{\tan y} = \cos y\) and \(\frac{1}{\tan y} = \cot y\). Rearranged,
\(\frac{dx}{dy} + (\cot y)\,x = \cos y\),
which is linear in \(x\) with \(P = \cot y\) and \(Q = \cos y\).
The integrating factor is
\(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \cot y\,dy} = e^{\log \sin y} = \sin y\).
The solution is therefore
\(x\,(\sin y) = \int \cos y \cdot \sin y\,dy\).
Substituting \(u = \sin y\), \(du = \cos y\,dy\), the right side is \(\int u\,du = \frac{u^2}{2}\), so
\(x \sin y = \frac{\sin^2 y}{2} + C\).
Applying \(y(0) = 0\), i.e. \(y = 0\) when \(x = 0\): \(0 = 0 + C\), so \(C = 0\).
Hence the particular solution is
\(x \sin y = \frac{\sin^2 y}{2}\),
and dividing by \(\sin y\) (legitimate wherever \(\sin y \ne 0\)) this simplifies to
\(\sin y = 2x\), that is \(y = \sin^{-1}(2x)\).
Check: from \(\sin y = 2x\) we get \(\cos y\,dy = 2\,dx\), and substituting into \((x - \sin y)dy + \tan y\,dx\) gives \(\left(\frac{\sin y}{2} - \sin y\right)dy + \tan y \cdot \frac{\cos y\,dy}{2} = -\frac{\sin y}{2}dy + \frac{\sin y}{2}dy = 0\), as required.
